title: Shopping & money
goal: Ask prices, bargain politely, choose between 'this one' and 'that one', and pay.
intro:
Kerala shopping ranges from huge textile showrooms to tiny corner shops and fish markets. Fixed prices are normal in shops; gentle bargaining is fine in markets and with street vendors. Digital payments (UPI — 'GPay') are everywhere, even at tea stalls.

This unit teaches the demonstratives — **ഈ / ആ** 'this / that' before a noun, and **ഇത് / അത്** 'this one / that one' — and the two different verbs for 'give': **തരുക** (give to me/us) and **കൊടുക്കുക** (give to someone else).

vocab.en: to take; to pick up; (shop) to buy
to look; to look after; to try
vocab.note: Past: നോക്കി. After another verb: 'try doing' (ഇട്ടുനോക്കുക 'try on').

vocab.en: right fit; right amount; cooked/ripe state
just, for nothing; free; in vain

phrases.en: How much is this? (lit. what price for this?)
The price is a bit high.
Could you lower it a little?

grammar.title: This and that: ഈ / ആ and ഇത് / അത്
grammar.body:
Malayalam builds demonstratives on **ഇ-** (near) and **അ-** (far), with **എ-** for the question word:

• before a noun: **ഈ** *ī* 'this', **ആ** *ā* 'that', **ഏത്** *ētŭ* 'which': ഈ സാരി 'this saree', ആ കട 'that shop', ഏത് ബസ്? 'which bus?'
• standing alone ('this one'): **ഇത്** *itŭ*, **അത്** *atŭ*, **ഏത്** *ētŭ*: ഇത് വേണം 'I want this one'. Plural: ഇവ / അവ (things, formal) — in speech usually ഇതൊക്കെ 'all these'.
• place: ഇവിടെ / അവിടെ / എവിടെ; manner: ഇങ്ങനെ 'like this' / അങ്ങനെ 'like that' / എങ്ങനെ 'how'.

'This one or that one?' = **ഇതോ അതോ?** (-ഓ … -ഓ = 'or' in questions). 'This very one' = **ഇതുതന്നെ**.

examples.en: Could you show me that red saree?
This one or that one — which is better?
I don't want that one; this one will do.

grammar.title: Prices and giving: dative 'for', തരുക vs കൊടുക്കുക
grammar.body:
Price questions use the **dative** ('for this'): ഇതി**ന്** എന്താ വില? 'what's the price for this?', ഒരു കിലോയ്**ക്ക്** എത്രയാ? 'how much for a kilo?'. The amount paid also takes the dative: നൂറ് രൂപ**യ്ക്ക്** തരാമോ? 'will you give it for 100 rupees?'.

Malayalam has **two verbs for 'give'**, depending on direction:
• **തരുക** *taruka* — give **towards the speaker** (to me / us): ഒരു ബാഗ് **തരൂ** 'give me a bag'.
• **കൊടുക്കുക** *koṭukkuka* — give **to anyone else** (you, him, them): ഞാൻ കാശ് **കൊടുത്തു** 'I gave (him) the money'.

Using കൊടുക്കുക when you mean 'give me' sounds wrong to a native ear.

examples.en: How much for a kilo of fish?
Will you give it (to me) for 200 rupees?

dialogue.title: Buying a mundu
dialogue.setting: Peter shops for a mundu (traditional wrap) for Onam in a textile shop in Thrissur.

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.en: Come in, sir, what would you like?

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.native: എനിക്ക് ഒരു കസവ് മുണ്ട് വേണം, ഓണത്തിന്.
lines.roman: enikkŭ oru kasavŭ muṇḍŭ vēṇam, ōṇattinŭ.
lines.en: I'd like a kasavu mundu, for Onam.

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.en: Here, look at this. It's good quality.

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.native: കുറച്ച് കൂടുതലാണ്. വേറെ ഉണ്ടോ, കുറച്ച് വിലക്കുറവുള്ളത്?
lines.roman: kuṟacchŭ kūṭutalāṇŭ. vēṟe uṇḍō, kuṟacchŭ vilakkuṟavuḷḷatŭ?
lines.en: That's a bit much. Is there another, a bit cheaper?

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.en: Yes. This mundu is five hundred rupees.

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.en: This one or that one? Which is better?

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.en: The first one is better. For you, sir, I'll give it for 750.

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.native: ശരി, ഞാൻ അത് എടുക്കാം. ജിപേ ചെയ്യാമോ?
lines.roman: shari, ñān atŭ eṭukkām. jipē cheyyāmō?
lines.en: OK, I'll take that one. Can I pay by GPay?

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.en: Yes, sir. Here's the QR code.

culture: The **kasavu** (cream cotton with a gold border) mundu for men and saree or set-mundu for women is Kerala's festive dress, worn especially at Onam and Vishu. Men often fold the mundu up to the knee when walking — but fold it down when greeting elders or entering a temple. Textile showrooms are huge, air-conditioned and famous for their advertising; small shops give 'loose' items in paper bags because plastic is restricted.
